description: Each gender's volume is its number of distinct orders that have at least one invoice.

a.request: Linking each invoice to its order and that order's customer (dropping invoices without a matching order or customer), count for each customer gender (`Customers.gender`) the number of distinct orders that have at least one invoice, counting each such order once however many invoices it has. Work out each gender's share as its count divided by the total of the counts over all genders, and average these shares across the genders. Return only the genders whose share is above that average, showing the gender, the count, the share, and the share minus the average share, without rounding.
a.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS cnt FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON i.order_id = o.order_id JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), s AS (SELECT gender, cnt, CAST(cnt AS REAL) / (SELECT SUM(cnt) FROM g) AS share FROM g), a AS (SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT s.gender, s.cnt AS count, s.share AS share, s.share - a.avg_share AS diff_from_average FROM s, a WHERE s.share > a.avg_share

b.request: For each customer gender in `Customers.gender`, count the distinct orders that have at least one invoice (joining Invoices to Orders to Customers via inner joins and dropping unlinked rows), compute each gender's share as its count divided by the total count across all genders, and list only the genders whose share exceeds the average share across genders, showing gender, count, share, and share minus average share, with no rounding
b.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS cnt FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON i.order_id = o.order_id JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), s AS (SELECT gender, cnt, cnt * 1.0 / SUM(cnt) OVER () AS share FROM g), a AS (SELECT gender, cnt, share, AVG(share) OVER () AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT gender, cnt AS count, share, share - avg_share AS share_minus_avg_share FROM a WHERE share > avg_share

c.request: Going from invoices to their orders and on to the customers (skip anything that doesn't link up), how many invoiced orders does each customer gender (`Customers.gender`) have? Turn that into each gender's share of the overall total, and list the genders whose share is above the average share across genders: give the gender, the count, the share, and how far the share sits above the average. Don't round anything. Each gender's volume is its number of distinct orders that have at least one invoice.
c.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS cnt FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), s AS (SELECT gender, cnt, CAST(cnt AS REAL) / (SELECT SUM(cnt) FROM g) AS share FROM g), a AS (SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT s.gender, s.cnt AS order_count, s.share AS share, s.share - a.avg_share AS share_above_average FROM s CROSS JOIN a WHERE s.share > a.avg_share

d.request: Going from invoices to their orders and on to the customers (skipping anything that doesn't link up), what is each customer gender's (`Customers.gender`) volume, defined as its number of distinct orders that have at least one invoice? Turn that into each gender's share of the overall total, and list the genders whose share is above the average share across genders, giving the gender, the count, the share, and how far the share sits above the average. Don't round anything.
d.sql: WITH v AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON i.order_id = o.order_id JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), s AS (SELECT gender, order_count, order_count * 1.0 / SUM(order_count) OVER () AS share FROM v), a AS (SELECT gender, order_count, share, AVG(share) OVER () AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT gender, order_count, share, share - avg_share AS share_above_average FROM a WHERE share > avg_share
